presentation_slides.title: What is Physics?
content: Physics is a science that generates fundamental knowledge needed for future technological advances.
It drives the economic engines of the world by contributing to technological infrastructure.
Physics provides the foundational understanding for other disciplines like chemistry, engineering, and biomedical sciences.

presentation_slides.title: Physics and Technology
content: Modern conveniences like television, computers, and phones are possible due to physics discoveries.
Modern transportation (aircraft, automobiles, space shuttles) relies on physics.
Simple mechanical devices (pulleys, levers) and complex machines (quantum computers, nuclear reactors) are created using physics.

presentation_slides.title: Everyday Objects and Physics
content: Many ordinary objects rely on physics to function:
- Semiconductors
- Lasers
- X-rays
- GPS devices
- Radio transmitters
- Bar code scanners

presentation_slides.title: Physics in Medicine
content: Physics improves quality of life through medical applications:
- Computer Tomography (CT)
- Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
- Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
- Ultrasonic imaging
- Laser surgery

presentation_slides.title: Physics and Global Challenges
content: Physics plays an important role in developing strategies to combat climate change.
It contributes to the development of cleaner energies.
Physics and technology must work together to resolve the need for new technologies that decrease damage to our planet.
Physics helps develop solutions for deadly diseases and resource management.

presentation_slides.title: What are Physics Communities?
content: Physics communities are organized groups of persons associated together for scientific purposes.
They are established at national, continental, and worldwide levels.
They aim to promote physics education, research, and collaboration.

presentation_slides.title: Ethiopian Physical Society (EPS)
content: Established by Ethiopian physics professionals to enhance physics research and education in Ethiopia.
Objectives include:
- Promoting physics education and research
- Organizing conferences and exchanging scientific information
- Popularizing physics to make students develop interest
- Contributing to the design and implementation of the physics curriculum
- Creating means for disseminating scientific information

presentation_slides.title: Other Physics Communities
content: Ethiopian Physics Society in North America (EPSNA):
- Promotes physics education and research among Ethiopians in Ethiopia and North America.
- Donates educational materials, field equipment, computing facilities, and provides scholarships.
African Association of Physics Students (aaps):
- Student-run educational association.
- Encourages physics students in their scientific and professional work.
- Promotes relations between physics students from all over the world.

presentation_slides.title: Sources of Knowledge
content: A Posteriori Knowledge: Knowledge through experience (seeing, hearing, feeling).
- Sensory perception, introspection, memory, and testimony.
A Priori Knowledge: Knowledge that does not come from experience.
- Derived from reason itself, such as logical and mathematical truths.

presentation_slides.title: The Scientific Method
content: An ordered series of steps to acquire knowledge based on experimental evidence.
Steps:
1. Observation
2. Question
3. Research
4. Hypothesis
5. Experiment
6. Analysis
7. Conclusion

presentation_slides.title: Scientific Method Example
content: Observation: Water boiled at a lower temperature in the mountains.
Question: Why does water boil at different temperatures?
Research: Boiling temperature depends on molecular bonds and pressure.
Hypothesis: Atmospheric pressure changes with altitude, affecting boiling temperature.
Experiment: Heat water at different altitudes and record the boiling temperature.
Analysis: Data shows boiling temperature decreases with increasing altitude.
Conclusion: The original hypothesis was correct.

sections.section_title: The Mission of Physics and Career Awareness

presentation_slides.title: Mission of Physics
content: The mission of physics is to advance science, engineering, and innovation throughout the world for the benefit of all.
Serving society is a core part of the mission.

presentation_slides.title: Careers in Physics
content: Physics graduates have skills in high demand:
- Numeracy
- Problem-solving
- Data analysis
- Communication of complex ideas
Career opportunities exist in education, automotive, aerospace, defense, public sector, healthcare, energy, materials, technology, computing, and IT.

presentation_slides.title: Physics Careers in Space, Astronomy, and Healthcare
content: Space and Astronomy: Study the universe, collect data from satellites and telescopes.
Healthcare: Medical physics overlaps with biomedical engineering. Areas include radiology, radiation oncology, and nuclear medicine.

presentation_slides.title: Physics Careers in Engineering, Energy, and Technology
content: Engineering: Improve and develop products and manufacturing processes.
Energy: Work in renewable and non-renewable energy sectors (oil, gas, wind, solar).
Technology: Work in robotics, nanoscience, and nanotechnology.

presentation_slides.title: Recent Discoveries in Physics
content: Physics is the study of the physical world, from the smallest particles to galaxies and black holes.
Recent discoveries include: Exoplanets, Black holes, Quantum cryptography, Higgs boson, Gravitational waves, Global warming modeling, and the James Webb Space Telescope.

presentation_slides.title: Exoplanets and Black Holes
content: Exoplanets: Planets outside our solar system.
- As of October 2022, there are 5,197 confirmed exoplanets.
- Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery.
Black Holes: Regions of spacetime with such strong gravity that nothing can escape.
- Roger Penrose, Reinhard Genzel, and Andrea M. Ghez won the 2020 Nobel Prize for black hole discoveries.

presentation_slides.title: Quantum Cryptography and Higgs Boson
content: Quantum Cryptography: An application of quantum physics that enhances the security of information exchange.
Higgs Boson: A subatomic particle.
- Discovered on July 4, 2012, by CERN scientists.
- The experiment took 60 years to prove the existence of this particle.

presentation_slides.title: Gravitational Waves and Global Warming
content: Gravitational Waves: Waves in spacetime that travel at the speed of light.
- Hypothesized by Einstein in 1916.
- Proved to be right in 2016 by LIGO.
Global Warming: Increase in Earth's temperature and its impact on climate.
- Syukuro Manabe and Klaus Hasselmann won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for modeling Earth's climate.

presentation_slides.title: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Future Perspectives
content: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST): An infrared telescope located 1.5 million km beyond Earth's orbit.
- It will tell us about the assembly of galaxies, birth of stars, and exoplanets.
Future Perspectives: Research at the forefront is very expensive and requires international collaboration.
Developing countries like Ethiopia must start doing physics at the highest level for national security and sustainable growth.

presentation_slides.title: Scalars and Vectors
content: Scalars: Physical quantities that have only magnitude (size) and unit.
- Examples: mass, speed, distance, density, volume.
Vectors: Physical quantities that have both magnitude and direction.
- Examples: force, velocity, acceleration, displacement.

presentation_slides.title: Graphical Representation of Vectors
content: A vector is represented graphically by an arrow:
- The length of the arrow represents the magnitude (drawn to scale).
- The tip of the arrow represents the direction of the vector.
A scale is used similar to maps (e.g., 1 cm = 10 km).

presentation_slides.title: Types of Vectors
content: Parallel Vectors: Vectors in the same direction.
Antiparallel Vectors: Vectors in opposite directions.
Equal Vectors: Vectors with the same magnitude and direction.
Collinear Vectors: Vectors that lie along the same line or parallel lines.
Coplanar Vectors: Three or more vectors lying in the same plane.
Zero Vector: A vector with zero magnitude.
Orthogonal Vectors: Vectors that are perpendicular.
Unit Vector: A vector with a magnitude of exactly one unit.
Negative of a Vector: Same magnitude, opposite direction.

sections.section_title: Graphical Method of Addition of Vectors in Two Dimensions (2-D)

presentation_slides.title: Graphical Vector Addition
content: Graphical methods provide a visual understanding of vectors.
Vectors must have the same units to be added.
Translation of a vector: Moving it parallel to itself without changing magnitude or direction.
The result of adding vectors is called the resultant vector.

presentation_slides.title: Triangle Law of Vector Addition
content: Place the vectors head-to-tail.
The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector.
The order of addition does not matter (commutative): A + B = B + A

presentation_slides.title: Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition
content: Place the vectors tail-to-tail.
Construct a parallelogram using the vectors as sides.
The resultant vector is the diagonal drawn from the tails to the opposite corner.

presentation_slides.title: Polygon Law of Vector Addition and Subtraction
content: Polygon Law: Used for more than two vectors.
- Place vectors head-to-tail in sequence.
- The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the last.
Subtraction of Vectors: Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative.

sections.section_title: Algebraic Method of addition of vectors in Two Dimensions (2-D)

presentation_slides.title: Algebraic Vector Addition
content: Algebraic methods provide exact results compared to graphical methods.
They use trigonometric functions to find the resultant.
Adding Collinear Vectors:
- Same direction: Add magnitudes.
- Opposite directions: Subtract magnitudes.

presentation_slides.title: Adding Perpendicular Vectors
content: Magnitude: Use the Pythagorean theorem.
- R = √(A² + B²)
Direction: Use trigonometry.
- tan θ = (opposite side) / (adjacent side)
The angle is measured from a reference direction.

presentation_slides.title: Components of a Vector
content: A vector can be resolved into its x and y components.
Ax = A cos θ (x-component)
Ay = A sin θ (y-component)
The components are projections of the vector onto the coordinate axes.
Resolution of a vector is the process of breaking it into its components.

presentation_slides.title: Component Method of Vector Addition
content: This is the most general method for adding vectors.
Resolve each vector into its x and y components.
Sum the x-components to get the resultant's x-component (Rx = ΣAx).
Sum the y-components to get the resultant's y-component (Ry = ΣAy).
Magnitude of the resultant: R = √(Rx² + Ry²).
Direction: θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx).

presentation_slides.title: Unit Vectors
content: A unit vector has a magnitude of exactly one.
It indicates direction only.
î (i-hat): unit vector in the positive x-direction.
ĵ (j-hat): unit vector in the positive y-direction.
A vector can be written as: A = Ax î + Ay ĵ.
The unit vector along a vector A is U_A = A / |A|.

presentation_slides.title: Multiplying a Vector by a Scalar
content: Multiplying a vector A by a scalar c gives a new vector.
Magnitude: |c| times the magnitude of A.
Direction: If c > 0, the direction is the same as A. If c < 0, the direction is opposite to A.

presentation_slides.title: The Dot (Scalar) Product
content: The dot product of two vectors A and B is a scalar quantity.
Definition: A·B = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between them (placed tail-to-tail).
The result is a number (scalar) with no direction.
Alternative definition: A·B = AxBx + AyBy.

presentation_slides.title: Applications of the Dot Product
content: The dot product can be positive (θ < 90°), negative (θ > 90°), or zero (θ = 90°).
If A·B = 0, then A and B are perpendicular.
Work: W = F·d (force applied through a displacement).
Power: P = F·v (force applied to an object moving with velocity).

chapters.chapter_title: Motion in One and Two Dimensions

presentation_slides.title: What is Acceleration?
content: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
It is a vector quantity.
SI unit: m/s².
An object accelerates when its velocity changes in magnitude, direction, or both.

presentation_slides.title: Average and Instantaneous Acceleration
content: Average Acceleration: a_avg = (v_f - v_i) / Δt
- The change in velocity divided by the time interval.
Instantaneous Acceleration: acceleration at a specific instant.
- a_ins = lim (Δt → 0) Δv / Δt

presentation_slides.title: Understanding Acceleration Signs
content: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down (deceleration).
It depends on the sign of the velocity.
If velocity and acceleration have the same sign (both positive or both negative), the object is speeding up.
If they have opposite signs, the object is slowing down.

sections.section_title: Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion in 1D

presentation_slides.title: Kinematic Equations
content: These equations apply only to uniformly accelerated motion (constant acceleration).
Variables:
- s = displacement
- u or v_i = initial velocity
- v or v_f = final velocity
- a = acceleration
- t = time

presentation_slides.title: The Five Key Equations
content: 1. v_f = v_i + a t
2. v_avg = (v_i + v_f) / 2
4. s = v_i t + ½ a t²
5. v_f² = v_i² + 2 a s
These are vector equations, so sign convention must be consistent.

presentation_slides.title: Stopping Distance
content: Stopping distance is the total distance a vehicle travels from detecting a hazard to coming to a stop.
It is the sum of:
- Reaction Distance: distance traveled during the driver's reaction time.
s_r = v × t (reaction time)
- Braking Distance: distance traveled while braking.
s_b = v² / (2μg) where μ is the coefficient of friction.
Total Stopping Distance: s = v t + v² / (2μg)

sections.section_title: Graphical Representation of Uniformly accelerated Motion in 1 D

presentation_slides.title: Displacement-Time Graphs
content: Shows how displacement changes with time.
The slope of the graph gives the velocity.
- A flat line (zero slope) means the object is at rest.
- A straight line with a constant slope means constant velocity.
- A curved line means changing velocity (acceleration or deceleration).

presentation_slides.title: Velocity-Time Graphs
content: Shows how velocity changes with time.
The slope of the graph gives the acceleration.
- A flat line (zero slope) means constant velocity (zero acceleration).
- A straight line with a constant slope means constant acceleration.
The area under the graph gives the displacement.

presentation_slides.title: Acceleration-Time Graphs
content: Shows how acceleration changes with time.
For uniformly accelerated motion, the graph is a horizontal line at a constant value.
For uniform motion (zero acceleration), the graph is a line at a = 0.

presentation_slides.title: Summary of Graphical Analysis
content: Displacement-time graph slope = velocity.
Velocity-time graph slope = acceleration.
Velocity-time graph area under curve = displacement.
These relationships are fundamental for interpreting motion graphs.

presentation_slides.title: Free Fall
content: Free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone.
The acceleration is constant and is called the acceleration due to gravity (g).
Near the Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward.
All objects, regardless of mass, fall with the same acceleration (neglecting air resistance).

presentation_slides.title: Equations for Free Fall
content: The kinematic equations apply, with 'a' replaced by 'g'.
For upward motion (projected upward):
- v = u - gt
- y = ut - ½gt²
- v² = u² - 2gy
For downward motion (dropped from rest or thrown downward):
- v = u + gt
- y = ut + ½gt²

presentation_slides.title: Terminal Velocity
content: When an object falls through a fluid (like air), it experiences a drag force upward.
The drag force increases with speed.
Terminal velocity is reached when the upward drag force balances the downward weight.
At terminal velocity, the net force is zero, so acceleration is zero, and the object falls at a constant maximum speed.

presentation_slides.title: Uniform Circular Motion
content: An object moves in a circle at a constant speed.
The speed is constant, but the velocity is changing because its direction is constantly changing.
Changing direction means there is acceleration.
This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration (center-seeking).

presentation_slides.title: Angular and Tangential Quantities
content: Angular Displacement (θ): The angle swept out by the object.
- θ = s / r (where s is the arc length, r is the radius).
Angular Velocity (ω): The rate of change of angular displacement.
- ω = Δθ / Δt
Tangential Velocity (v_t): The linear speed along the circular path.
- v_t = r ω = 2πr / T (T is the period)

presentation_slides.title: Centripetal Acceleration and Force
content: Centripetal Acceleration (a_c): a_c = v²/r = ω²r.
It is always directed towards the center of the circle.
Centripetal Force (F_c): The net force causing centripetal acceleration.
- F_c = m a_c = m v²/r = m ω²r
This force is not a new type of force; it is the net force from other forces (tension, friction, gravity).

presentation_slides.title: Examples of Circular Motion
content: A ball on a string: Tension provides the centripetal force.
A car on a roundabout: Friction between tires and road provides the centripetal force.
A car on a banked road: The horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal force.
The conical pendulum: The horizontal component of tension provides the centripetal force.

sections.section_title: The Concept of Force and Newton's Laws of motion

presentation_slides.title: The Concept of Force
content: A force is a push or a pull.
It is a vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction.
SI unit: Newton (N).
A force can change the speed, direction, or shape of an object.

presentation_slides.title: Types of Forces
content: Contact Forces: Result from physical contact between two bodies.
- Examples: Friction, tension, normal force.
Field Forces: Act at a distance without physical contact.
- Examples: Gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic forces.
The four fundamental forces in nature are all field forces.

presentation_slides.title: Fundamental Forces in Nature
content: 1. Strong Nuclear Force: The strongest force; holds the nucleus together.
2. Electromagnetic Force: Acts between charged particles.
3. Weak Nuclear Force: Responsible for radioactive decay.
4. Gravitational Force: The weakest force; acts between all masses.

presentation_slides.title: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)
content: An object at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by an external net force.
An object in motion continues in straight-line motion at constant velocity unless acted upon by an external net force.
Inertia: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion.
Mass is a measure of inertia.

presentation_slides.title: Newton's Second Law
content: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force applied to it.
It is inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
Mathematically: F_net = m a
The direction of the acceleration is the same as the direction of the net force.

presentation_slides.title: Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction)
content: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.
The action and reaction forces act on different objects.
Example: When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force.
Action and reaction forces do not cancel each other because they act on different objects.

presentation_slides.title: Weight and Normal Force
content: Weight (W): The gravitational force on an object.
- W = m g
- It is directed downward toward the center of the Earth.
Normal Force (F_N): The perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on an object.
- On a level surface, F_N = W (if no other vertical forces).
- On an inclined plane, F_N = W cos θ.

presentation_slides.title: What is Friction?
content: Friction is a force that opposes the motion (or attempted motion) of one surface over another.
It arises due to the roughness of the surfaces in contact.
Friction is a contact force.
It has both beneficial and detrimental effects.

presentation_slides.title: Types of Friction
content: Static Friction (F_s): The friction between surfaces at rest relative to each other.
- It can take any value from zero up to a maximum value.
- F_s,max = μ_s F_N
Kinetic Friction (F_k): The friction between surfaces sliding over each other.
- F_k = μ_k F_N
Generally, μ_s > μ_k, so static friction is greater than kinetic friction.

presentation_slides.title: Coefficient of Friction
content: The coefficient of friction (μ) is the ratio of the frictional force to the normal force.
- μ = F_f / F_N
It is a dimensionless number that depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact.
It does not depend on the area of contact.

presentation_slides.title: Applications of Friction
content: Friction is essential for walking, driving, and holding objects.
Without friction, car tires would not grip the road.
Friction can be reduced by using lubricants (oil, grease).
Friction causes energy loss as heat and causes wear and tear.

presentation_slides.title: Free-Body Diagrams
content: A free-body diagram is a drawing that shows all the forces acting on a single object.
It is essential for applying Newton's Laws to solve problems.
Steps:
- Draw the object.
- Draw each force as an arrow acting on the object.
- Label each force.
- Resolve forces into x and y components if needed.

presentation_slides.title: Translational Equilibrium
content: An object is in translational equilibrium when its acceleration is zero.
This means it is either at rest or moving with constant velocity.
The net force acting on the object must be zero.

presentation_slides.title: The First Condition of Equilibrium
content: The vector sum of all forces acting on an object in equilibrium must be zero.
ΣF = 0
This can be written in component form:
- ΣFx = 0
- ΣFy = 0
These equations can be used to solve for unknown forces in static situations.

presentation_slides.title: Work
content: Work is done when a force acts on an object and causes a displacement.
Work is the transfer of energy.
Definition: W = F·d = F d cos θ
SI unit: Joule (J).
Work can be positive, negative, or zero.
- Positive: Force and displacement are in the same direction.
- Negative: Force and displacement are in opposite directions (e.g., friction).
- Zero: Force and displacement are perpendicular.

presentation_slides.title: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
content: Kinetic Energy (KE): The energy an object has due to its motion.
- KE = ½ m v²
The Work-Energy Theorem: The net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy.
- W_net = ΔKE = ½ m v_f² - ½ m v_i²

presentation_slides.title: Potential Energy
content: Potential Energy (PE): Stored energy.
Gravitational Potential Energy: Energy due to an object's height above a reference point.
- PE_g = m g h
Elastic Potential Energy: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring.
- PE_s = ½ k x² (where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement from equilibrium)

presentation_slides.title: Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces
content: Conservative Forces: The work done by the force is independent of the path taken.
- Examples: Gravity, spring force.
- The work done around any closed path is zero.
Non-Conservative Forces: The work done depends on the path.
- Examples: Friction, air resistance.
- These forces convert mechanical energy into other forms (like heat).

presentation_slides.title: Power
content: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
Average Power: P_avg = W / t
Instantaneous Power: P = dW / dt = F·v
SI unit: Watt (W). 1 W = 1 J/s.

presentation_slides.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
content: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy: E = KE + PE.
In the absence of non-conservative forces (like friction), the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved.
This means: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f
Energy can transform between KE and PE, but the total remains constant.

presentation_slides.title: Applications of Energy Conservation
content: This principle is a powerful tool for solving problems.
It relates speeds and heights without considering the details of the motion.
Examples:
- A roller coaster in a frictionless track.
- An object in free fall.
- A pendulum swinging without air resistance.

presentation_slides.title: Linear Momentum
content: Linear momentum (p) is the product of an object's mass and velocity.
p = m v
It is a vector quantity.
SI unit: kg·m/s.
Momentum describes how difficult it is to stop or set an object in motion.

presentation_slides.title: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem
content: Impulse (J) is the product of the net force acting on an object and the time interval over which it acts.
J = F_net Δt
The Impulse-Momentum Theorem: The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum.
J = Δp = m v_f - m v_i
This theorem is a direct consequence of Newton's Second Law.

presentation_slides.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
content: The Law of Conservation of Momentum: The total momentum of an isolated system (no external forces) remains constant.
p_initial = p_final
For two objects: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2
This applies to all types of collisions, regardless of whether energy is conserved.

presentation_slides.title: Types of Collisions
content: Elastic Collisions: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Inelastic Collisions: Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.
Perfectly Inelastic Collisions: A special case where the objects stick together after collision.
- They move with the same final velocity.
- Maximum kinetic energy is lost.

presentation_slides.title: Center of Mass
content: The center of mass is the point where the total mass of a system can be considered to be concentrated.
It is the average position of all the mass in the system.
For a system of particles, the velocity of the center of mass is given by:
- v_cm = (Σ m_i v_i) / M_total
The center of mass moves as if all the external forces act on it and all mass is concentrated there.

presentation_slides.title: Heat and Temperature
content: Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects due to a temperature difference.
It always flows spontaneously from a hotter object to a colder object.
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Heat is a process variable (energy in transit), while temperature is a state variable.

presentation_slides.title: Internal Energy
content: Internal energy is the total energy stored within a system.
It includes the kinetic energy of particle motion (translational, rotational, vibrational) and the potential energy from intermolecular forces.
When heat is added to a system, its internal energy increases (usually raising its temperature).
Work can also change the internal energy of a system.

presentation_slides.title: Conduction
content: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material by molecular collisions.
Energy is transferred from high-energy particles to low-energy particles.
It is most effective in solids, especially metals (good conductors).
Insulators (e.g., wood, wool) conduct heat poorly.

presentation_slides.title: Convection
content: Convection is the transfer of heat by the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas).
It occurs due to differences in density.
- Warm fluid is less dense and rises.
- Cool fluid is denser and sinks.
This creates a convection current.
Examples: Boiling water, heating a room.

presentation_slides.title: Radiation
content: Radiation is the transfer of heat via electromagnetic waves.
It does not require a medium; it can travel through a vacuum.
All objects emit and absorb thermal radiation.
Examples: Heat from the Sun, heat from a fire.

sections.section_title: Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity

presentation_slides.title: Heat Capacity
content: Heat Capacity (C): The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of an object by 1°C or 1 K.
C = Q / ΔT
SI unit: J/K.
Heat capacity depends on the object's mass and the material it is made of.

presentation_slides.title: Specific Heat Capacity
content: Specific Heat Capacity (c): The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C or 1 K.
c = Q / (m ΔT)
SI unit: J/(kg·K).
It is an intrinsic property of the material.
Different substances have different specific heat capacities.

presentation_slides.title: Specific Heat Values and Significance
content: Metals tend to have low specific heat (e.g., lead, copper).
Water has a very high specific heat (4186 J/kg·K).
This is why water is used as a coolant.
It also moderates coastal climates, as oceans absorb and release large amounts of heat without large temperature changes.

presentation_slides.title: Thermal Expansion
content: Thermal expansion is the change in size of matter in response to a change in temperature.
Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled.
Gases expand much more than liquids, and liquids expand more than solids.

presentation_slides.title: Linear, Area, and Volume Expansion
content: Linear Expansion: ΔL = L₀ α ΔT
- α is the coefficient of linear expansion.
Area (Surface) Expansion: ΔA = A₀ β ΔT
- β = 2α
Volume Expansion: ΔV = V₀ γ ΔT
- γ = 3α

presentation_slides.title: Applications and Anomalies
content: Applications: Bimetallic strips (thermostats), riveting, fitting metal parts.
Water has a unique expansion property.
Its volume decreases as temperature rises from 0°C to 4°C.
This is why ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down.

presentation_slides.title: Phase Changes
content: A phase change is a transition between solid, liquid, and gas states.
During a phase change, the temperature of the substance does not change.
Energy supplied during a phase change is used to change the arrangement of molecules, not their average kinetic energy.
This energy is called latent heat.

presentation_slides.title: Latent Heat
content: Latent Heat of Fusion (L_f): The heat required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point.
Q = m L_f
Latent Heat of Vaporization (L_v): The heat required to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point.
Q = m L_v
Examples: Melting ice, boiling water.

presentation_slides.title: Phase Diagram
content: A phase diagram is a graph of pressure vs. temperature showing the conditions for different phases.
Triple Point: Where all three phases (solid, liquid, gas) coexist in equilibrium.
Critical Point: Where the liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable.

presentation_slides.title: What is Calorimetry?
content: Calorimetry is the measurement of heat exchange between substances.
It is based on the principle of conservation of energy.
In an isolated system: Heat lost by hot objects = Heat gained by cold objects.
A device used for this is called a calorimeter.

presentation_slides.title: Method of Mixtures
content: A hot object is placed in a calorimeter with cold water.
The final equilibrium temperature is measured.
By equating the heat lost by the hot object to the heat gained by the water and calorimeter, the specific heat capacity of the hot object can be calculated.
Equation: m_s c_s (T_s - T_f) = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c) (T_f - T_c)

presentation_slides.title: Electrical Method
content: An electrical heater of known power is used to heat a substance.
The electrical energy supplied is: E = P t
This is equated to the heat gained by the substance: Q = m c ΔT.
This method is used to determine the specific heat capacity of solids and liquids.

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Latent Heat
content: Calorimetry can also be used to measure latent heats.
For example, to measure the latent heat of fusion of ice:
- Add a known mass of ice to warm water in a calorimeter.
- Measure the temperature drop of the water.
- Equate the heat lost by the water to the heat gained by the ice (to melt and warm to the final temperature).
A similar method can be used for the latent heat of vaporization of steam.

presentation_slides.title: Electric Charge
content: Charge is a fundamental property of matter.
There are two types: Positive (proton) and Negative (electron).
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
Charge is quantized: q = n e, where e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Charge is conserved.

presentation_slides.title: Coulomb's Law
content: Coulomb's Law describes the force between two point charges.
F = k |q₁ q₂| / r²
- k is Coulomb's constant (8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²).
The force is attractive for opposite charges and repulsive for like charges.
The force is a vector, acting along the line connecting the charges.

presentation_slides.title: Superposition Principle
content: When multiple charges are present, the net force on any one charge is the vector sum of the forces exerted on it by all the other charges.
This is the principle of superposition.
F_net = F₁₂ + F₁₃ + ... + F₁ₙ
Use vector addition to find the net force.

presentation_slides.title: Electric Field
content: An electric field exists around any charged object.
It is defined as the electric force per unit charge.
E = F / q (for a positive test charge q).
SI unit: N/C or V/m.
The electric field is a vector field, having both magnitude and direction.

presentation_slides.title: Field Lines
content: Electric field lines are used to visualize the field.
Properties:
- Lines originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges.
- Lines never cross.
- The density of lines indicates the strength of the field.
- Lines are perpendicular to the surface of conductors.
For a point charge: E = kQ/r².

presentation_slides.title: Electric Flux
content: Electric flux (Φ) is a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through a surface.
Φ = E·A = E A cos θ
The area vector is perpendicular to the surface.
Flux is maximum when the field is perpendicular to the surface (θ = 0).
Flux is zero when the field is parallel to the surface (θ = 90°).

presentation_slides.title: Electric Potential Energy and Potential
content: Electric potential energy (U) is the energy a charge has due to its position in an electric field.
Electric potential (V) is the potential energy per unit charge.
V = U / q
SI unit: Volt (V) = J/C.
Unlike the electric field (a vector), electric potential is a scalar quantity.

presentation_slides.title: Potential Difference
content: Potential difference (voltage) between two points is the work done per unit charge to move a charge between those points.
ΔV = ΔU / q = W / q
The potential due to a point charge: V = kQ/r.
The potential difference in a uniform electric field: ΔV = E d.

presentation_slides.title: Equipotential Surfaces
content: Equipotential surfaces connect points with the same electric potential.
No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to electric field lines.
For a point charge, equipotential surfaces are spheres.

sections.section_title: Electric Current, Resistance and ohm's law

presentation_slides.title: Electric Current
content: Electric current is the flow of electric charge.
I = ΔQ / Δt
SI unit: Ampere (A). 1 A = 1 C/s.
Conventional current flows from positive to negative.
Electrons flow from negative to positive.

presentation_slides.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance
content: Resistance (R) is the opposition to current flow.
SI unit: Ohm (Ω).
Ohm's Law: For ohmic conductors, V = I R.
A conductor obeys Ohm's law if the current is directly proportional to the voltage.

presentation_slides.title: Resistors in Series
content: Resistors connected end-to-end.
The same current flows through each resistor.
The total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + ...
The voltage is divided among the resistors.

presentation_slides.title: Resistors in Parallel
content: Resistors connected across the same potential difference.
The same voltage is across each resistor.
The total current is the sum of the currents through each resistor.
The total resistance is found by:
The total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistor.

presentation_slides.title: Kirchhoff's Rules
content: For complex circuits, use Kirchhoff's rules.
Junction Rule (Current Rule): The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it.
- ΣI_in = ΣI_out
Loop Rule (Voltage Rule): The sum of all potential changes around a closed loop is zero.
- ΣΔV = 0
These rules are based on conservation of charge and energy.

presentation_slides.title: Capacitors
content: A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge and energy.
It consists of two conductors (plates) separated by an insulator.
Charge is stored on the plates.
Circuit symbol:

presentation_slides.title: Capacitance
content: Capacitance (C) is the ratio of the charge stored to the potential difference.
C = Q / V
SI unit: Farad (F). 1 F = 1 C/V.
Practical units: μF, nF, pF.
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is: C = ε₀ A / d.

presentation_slides.title: Dielectrics
content: A dielectric is an insulating material placed between the plates.
It increases the capacitance by a factor of κ (the dielectric constant).
C = κ C₀
Dielectrics also increase the maximum voltage the capacitor can withstand.

presentation_slides.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
content: Capacitors in Parallel:
- The same voltage is across each.
- The total charge is the sum of the charges.
- C_eq = C₁ + C₂ + ...
Capacitors in Series:
- The same charge is on each.
- The total voltage is the sum of the voltages.

presentation_slides.title: Structure of the Nucleus
content: The nucleus is at the center of the atom.
It contains protons (positive charge) and neutrons (neutral).
Protons and neutrons are collectively called nucleons.
Atomic Number (Z) = Number of protons.
Mass Number (A) = Number of protons + Number of neutrons.
Isotopes: Atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A).

presentation_slides.title: Nuclear Forces
content: The Strong Nuclear Force: The force that holds nucleons together.
- It is a very short-range force (≈10⁻¹⁵ m).
- It is much stronger than the electrostatic repulsion between protons.
The Weak Nuclear Force: Responsible for beta decay.

presentation_slides.title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
content: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its individual nucleons.
This difference in mass is called the mass defect (Δm).
The missing mass is converted into energy that holds the nucleus together.
Einstein's equation: E = (Δm) c²
This energy is the binding energy of the nucleus.
Binding Energy per Nucleon: Total binding energy / A. It is a measure of nuclear stability.

presentation_slides.title: Radioactive Decay
content: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of an unstable nucleus.
It occurs to make the nucleus more stable.
Types of radiation: Alpha (α), Beta (β), and Gamma (γ).

presentation_slides.title: Alpha (α) Radiation
content: Alpha particle: A helium-4 nucleus (⁴₂He).
High mass and charge (+2e).
High ionizing power.
Low penetrating power.
Stopped by a piece of paper or the outer layer of skin.

presentation_slides.title: Beta (β) Radiation
content: Beta-minus (β⁻): A high-speed electron.
Beta-plus (β⁺): A positron.
Moderate ionizing power.
Moderate penetrating power.
Stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum.

presentation_slides.title: Gamma (γ) Radiation
content: Gamma radiation: High-energy electromagnetic radiation.
No mass and no charge.
Low ionizing power.
High penetrating power.
Requires several centimeters of lead or meters of concrete to stop.

presentation_slides.title: Radioactive Decay Law
content: Radioactive decay is a random process.
Activity (A): The number of decays per second.
A = λ N, where λ is the decay constant.
N(t) = N₀ e^(-λt), the number of nuclei remaining after time t.
Half-life (T₁/₂): The time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay.

presentation_slides.title: Medical Applications
content: Radiotherapy: Using radiation to treat cancer.
- External: Gamma rays from a Cobalt-60 source.
- Internal (Brachytherapy): Placing a radioactive source inside the body.
Radioactive Tracers: Using isotopes to diagnose diseases.
- Example: Iodine-131 to examine thyroid function.

presentation_slides.title: Radioactive Dating
content: Using the known half-life of isotopes to determine the age of objects.
Carbon-14 Dating: For organic materials (up to ~50,000 years).
- Carbon-14 is produced in the atmosphere.
- Living organisms have a constant ratio of C-14 to C-12.
- When an organism dies, the ratio decreases as C-14 decays.
Other isotopes (Uranium-238, Potassium-40) are used for dating rocks.

presentation_slides.title: Nuclear Fission
content: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei.
Example: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ⁸⁹₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n + Energy
Fission releases a large amount of energy.
Chain Reaction: The neutrons released can cause further fission events.
Controlled in nuclear reactors to generate electricity.
Uncontrolled in nuclear weapons.

presentation_slides.title: Nuclear Fusion
content: Fusion is the combining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
Example: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + Energy
This is the process that powers the Sun and stars.
Fusion requires extremely high temperatures (millions of degrees).
It could be a source of clean energy but is very difficult to achieve.

sections.section_title: Safety Rules Against Hazards of Nuclear Radiation

presentation_slides.title: Radiation Hazards
content: Ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, gamma) can damage living cells.
It can ionize atoms and molecules, disrupting biological processes.
Effects can be acute (burns, radiation sickness) or long-term (cancer, genetic mutations).
Protection is essential for anyone working with or near radioactive materials.

presentation_slides.title: Principles of Radiation Protection
content: Time: Minimize the time spent near a radiation source.
Distance: Maximize the distance from the source.
- The dose decreases rapidly with distance.
Shielding: Use appropriate barriers to absorb radiation.
- Examples: Lead, concrete, water.
These principles are used to reduce exposure.

presentation_slides.title: Safe Handling of Radioactive Materials
content: Use tongs or forceps to handle sources.
Keep sources at arm's length, pointing away from the body.
Store sources in a designated, shielded container.
Wear appropriate personal protective equipment.
Follow strict procedures for disposal of radioactive waste.
Regular monitoring of radiation levels is required.
